spoken: Right now, you are moving around the Sun at about thirty kilometres a second.
But the speed isn't steady. In early January, Earth moves about one kilometre a second faster than in early July.
The rule behind that was found more than four hundred years ago, in old records of the planet Mars.
It began with an error of eight arcminutes, which is about a quarter of the width of the Moon.
This is the story of Kepler's second law, the rule of equal areas in equal times.
In the late fifteen hundreds, the best measurements of the sky came from a Danish nobleman, Tycho Brahe.
From fifteen seventy-six, on the island of Ven, he built Uraniborg, an observatory funded by the king.
There were no telescopes yet. Tycho measured by eye, with large quadrants and sextants.
His positions came close to one arcminute, which is a sixtieth of a degree.
For scale, the full Moon is about thirty-one arcminutes across.
Year after year, he recorded where the planets were. Mars was among them.
In fifteen ninety-seven he left Denmark, and soon he was working for the emperor, in Prague.
In February sixteen hundred, he was joined by a twenty-eight-year-old mathematician, Johannes Kepler.
Tycho guarded his data closely. He set Kepler to work on a single planet, Mars.
In October sixteen oh one, Tycho died after a short illness. Two days later, Kepler took over as imperial mathematician.
Tycho's heirs owned the observations, which would delay Kepler's book for years. But he had the Mars data.
Astronomers had long modelled the planets with circles. Even Copernicus, who put the Sun near the middle, used circles.
So Kepler began with a circle too, with the Sun off centre, and a point from which the motion looks steady.
Fitting it to Tycho's numbers meant one long calculation, over and over again.
Take pity on me, he wrote, who had to go through with at least seventy repetitions of it.
The model matched Tycho's positions of Mars to within two arcminutes.
But at other points in the orbit, it missed by up to eight.
Tycho's data was far too accurate for an error that size to be ignored.
These eight minutes alone, Kepler wrote, will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of astronomy.
Something in his model was wrong, either the circle or the way the planet moved along it.
Kepler wanted a physical cause. He imagined a force from the Sun, pushing the planets round, weaker with distance.
So, he reasoned, a planet's speed falls as its distance grows. Twice as far means half as fast.
To find where the planet would be, he'd have to add up its distance from the Sun all along the way.
By late sixteen oh two he had a shortcut, which was to measure the area swept by the line from the Sun.
Picture each day's motion as a thin triangle, whose height is the distance from the Sun, and whose base is the distance travelled.
If speed falls as distance grows, every day's triangle has the same area.
That's equal areas in equal times. Oddly, Kepler found this, the second law, before the first.
His speed rule only works for orbits that are nearly circles. The area rule works for every orbit.
Now he needed the shape. He tried egg-shaped ovals, again and again.
After about forty failed attempts, in late sixteen oh four, he tried an ellipse.
He had thought it too simple, because surely earlier astronomers wouldn't have missed it.
It fitted. He had even had the formula earlier, without seeing it. Ah, what a foolish bird I have been!
An ellipse has two special points, its foci. The Sun sits at one. The other is empty.
That's Kepler's first law, that a planet's orbit is an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.
Mars's ellipse is barely squashed. It's less than half a percent narrower than it is long.
But the Sun is well off centre, sitting more than nine percent of the way from the middle to the end.
Of the planets, only Mercury's orbit is more stretched. Kepler was lucky that his planet was Mars.
In sixteen oh nine he published it in a book called Astronomia nova, the New Astronomy.
So where is a planet on a given day? Kepler turned the area rule into an equation.
Time gives an angle, called M, that ticks round steadily, like the hand of a clock.
The planet's real place is set by another angle, called E. And a small letter e says how stretched the ellipse is.
Kepler's equation says that M equals big E, minus small e times the sine of big E.
No algebra can solve it for E. So in sixteen twenty-one, Kepler suggested guessing, then improving the guess.
For Mars, start with E equal to M, put each answer back in, and in four rounds the digits stop changing.
This animation solves it for every frame. Here's a stretched orbit, so the effect is easy to see.
Split one trip around into twelve equal stretches of time, and shade the area each one sweeps.
Near the Sun, the wedges are short and fat. Far away, they're long and thin.
Measure them, and each one is a twelfth of the ellipse, or eight point three percent.
But the distance travelled in each stretch is wildly different.
On this orbit, the planet moves four times faster at its closest point, perihelion, than at aphelion, its farthest.
Earth's orbit is much rounder. But the rule still holds.
Earth passes perihelion around the third of January, at a hundred and forty-seven point one million kilometres from the Sun,
and aphelion around the fourth of July, at a hundred and fifty-two point one million kilometres.
So it's fastest in January, at about thirty point three kilometres a second, and slowest in July, at about twenty-nine point three.
You can see it on the calendar. From the March equinox to the September one takes about a hundred and eighty-six days.
The other half of the year takes only about a hundred and seventy-nine, because Earth passes perihelion then, moving faster.
So in the north, spring and summer together last about a week longer than autumn and winter.
Mars swings more, from about twenty-six and a half kilometres a second near the Sun to about twenty-two at the far end.
Comets show it best. Halley's Comet dips to about zero point six astronomical units from the Sun, then swings out to about thirty-five.
One astronomical unit is Earth's average distance from the Sun.
At the far end, in December twenty twenty-three, it was crawling along at just zero point nine one kilometres a second.
At the two ends, speed times distance is the same. So near the Sun, it races along at about fifty-four kilometres a second.
Of its roughly seventy-five-year orbit, it spends only about two years closer to the Sun than Jupiter. It's due back in twenty sixty-one.
Kepler wasn't done. He wanted a rule that linked all the planets, not just one.
By his own account, the answer came to him on the eighth of March, sixteen eighteen.
Square a planet's time to go round. Cube its distance from the Sun. The ratio is the same for every planet.
Jupiter takes eleven point eight six years to go round. Squared, that's about a hundred and forty-one.
It's five point two astronomical units from the Sun. Cubed, that's about a hundred and forty-one again.
With Kepler's own numbers, all six known planets agree to within about two percent.
I first believed I was dreaming, he wrote.
This third law appeared in sixteen nineteen, in his book The Harmony of the World.
There, Kepler heard music in the orbits. Earth's turning speed, seen from the Sun, varies by about a semitone.
The Earth sings mee, fah, mee, he wrote, and you may hear misery and famine in the syllables.
In sixteen twenty-one, his Epitome gave the area law its modern form.
That year he also noted that the third law fits Jupiter's four bright moons.
But why should planets obey these rules at all? The answer came from Isaac Newton.
In sixteen eighty-four he proved that anything pulled toward a fixed centre sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
His proof, in the Principia of sixteen eighty-seven, is beautifully simple. Imagine the pull comes in short, sharp tugs.
With no pull, the planet goes straight, covering equal distances in equal times.
Each step makes a triangle with the Sun. The same base and the same height give the same area.
Now a tug toward the Sun bends the path. But it pulls only along the line to the Sun.
So the new triangle keeps the same base and the same height as before. So it has the same area again.
Make the tugs smaller and more frequent, and the path becomes a smooth orbit. The areas stay equal.
Notice that the proof never needed to know how strong the pull is. Any pull toward a centre will do.
Today we call this conservation of angular momentum.
The ellipse and the third law need more. They need a pull that weakens with the square of the distance, as gravity does.
Kepler never called these laws. That word first appeared in print in seventeen thirty-eight, in a book by Voltaire.
The tidy set of three came later still, in eighteen oh four.
First, a planet's orbit is an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.
Second, the line from the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.
Third, the period squared goes with the distance cubed.
And it's all because Kepler refused to ignore eight arcminutes.
So this January, when it's coldest in the north, remember that Earth is at its closest to the Sun, and moving fastest.
